title: The Fake Car Dealership Website Scam
hook: Imagine showing up at the dealership and finding out the dealer has no record of your payment.
description: FTC-documented pattern: Scammers are cloning real auto dealer websites to steal upfront payments. Learn how to protect yourself. Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/09/scammers-are-spoofing-car-dealership-websites-what-you-need-know

scenes.narration: Imagine showing up at the dealership and finding out the dealer has no record of your payment.
scenes.heading: A Disappointing Arrival
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: While the car-buying process can be stressful, whether you’re shopping online or in person, the thought of driving off the dealer’s lot with that sweet ride you’ve had your eyes on can be exhilarating. But imagine showing up at the dealership and finding out the dealer has no record of your order or your payment. And that there’s no shiny car waiting for you! That’s what’s happening to unwitting car buyers who’ve been duped by scammers impersonating a car dealership. How the scam works Scammers

How the scam works Scammers set up bogus car dealership websites to trick you into paying up front for a car you’ll never lay hands on. They clone a real auto dealer’s website — often using AI to do so — copying the brand logos, vehicle listings, and photos down to the last detail. How to avoid the scam Here’s how to protect yourself from scammers that clone auto dealership websites. Search online for the dealer’s name with words like “scam,” “review,” or “complaint.” Any negative hits that come up are a red flag. So go the extra mile — ask to see the car, and the dealership, in person. If they won’t let you, pump the brakes. If the car is too far for you to visit in person, tell the dealer you want to hire a mobile inspection service to check out the car.
